item.title: The Death of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Child Changed Her View of Nigeria
item.description:
The writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and her husband were spending the holidays at their home in Lagos, Nigeria, last December when one of their twin sons came down with what seemed to be a cold. The child, Nkanu, was 21 months old — “precious” and “a funny baby,” in the words of his father, Ivara Esege. He was still playful, but when he developed a fever, Esege, who is a physician, started him on antibiotics.

By New Year’s Day, Nkanu had not improved, so the couple took him to a local children’s hospital. Concerned that he might have atypical Kawasaki disease, a childhood illness that can lead to heart attacks and strokes, Esege also contacted Johns Hopkins Hospital, near the couple’s American home in suburban Maryland. Johns Hopkins agreed to take Nkanu as a patient, but doctors there asked for additional tests to make sure he was safe to travel. Adichie and Esege took Nkanu to Euracare, another hospital in Lagos, for the examination.

The child was sedated with Propofol, a common anesthetic, to keep him still during an M.R.I. of his brain. Adichie was waiting outside when a doctor hurried past her into the cath lab. It was alarming: Why was he rushing to the room where Nkanu was having his test done? She waited in “pure panic,” she said, until the doctor returned. “He was very calm and he said to me, ‘Well, look, they gave him too much Propofol,’” Adichie recalled. “Those were his exact words, which I will never forget until the day I die.”

Nkanu had gone into cardiac arrest. Within 24 hours — it is not clear exactly when — he was dead.

Adichie and Esege told me this story in July, at their home in Maryland. On the table, there was a tray of healthy snacks: bowls of fresh cherries, another bowl of seeds and dried fruit. Adichie, 48, was dressed in a plain, loosefitting dress, her hair combed into two simple braids. Esege, tall with a curly salt-and-pepper Afro, wore a yellow T-shirt and gym shorts. He is 57 and, like his wife, a native of Nigeria.

There was an easy choreography between the couple, but also a palpable weariness. Leading me to the dining room, where we spoke for several hours, they moved slowly, as if bereavement were a kind of arthritis, pain carried in the bones. The house was more than quiet. Their daughter, age 10, was at day camp, and the younger of the twin boys was upstairs, sleeping. (The couple asked The New York Times not to use their children’s names to protect their privacy.)

Adichie and Esege still struggle to understand how their child could have died so suddenly and inexplicably. They have urged a coroner’s court to conduct an inquest — and the court is doing so — in hopes that they can help other Nigerians who have been harmed by the country’s troubled health care system but lack the means and influence to push for change. They stress that they are not suing the hospital or the doctors and just want a better health care system.

“That’s the only thing we can try and do just to help,” Esege told me. “Hopefully someone else will not have to go through this.”

The pain of Nkanu’s death has complicated Adichie’s relationship with Nigeria. The country, with its mix of resilience, vibrancy, corruption and economic desperation, is a vivid milieu in her work, exerting a strong magnetic pull on characters who leave.

In her best-known novel, “Americanah,” the main character, Ifemelu, is a young Nigerian woman who, much like the author, comes to the United States to study and live, only to experience exhaustion and alienation that feels like “cement in her soul.” Nigeria, Adichie writes, was “where she was supposed to be, the only place she could sink her roots in without the constant urge to tug them out and shake off the soil.”

Now Adichie feels uprooted. “My feelings toward Nigeria have changed,” she said. Her son’s death was the first irrevocable loss, her native country the second.

Health care in Nigeria suffers from relatively low government support, limited infrastructure and an exodus of skilled workers. According to a recent estimate from the World Bank, Nigeria has 0.4 doctors for every 1,000 people (the figure is 3.7 in the United States).

But Adichie said she had confidence in Euracare, which she was told was run by international standards. “It was kind of paraded as one of the best hospitals in Lagos,” she explained.

As it happened, she knew the doctor who spoke to her outside the cath lab. His name was Tosin Majekodunmi, and she had met him while accompanying her parents to their annual checkups at Euracare.

“My father liked him very much,” Adichie said. “I did come to consider him a friend. When my father died, he was very kind and called me.”

According to Adichie, Dr. Majekodunmi told her the doctors had saved Nkanu and he was now stable: “He said, ‘But everything is OK now because we got him back.’ And I kind of felt — I felt really confused.”

She shook her head and spoke more slowly, her voice thick with tears. “I trusted him,” she said.

Dr. Majekodunmi did not respond to interview requests from The Times.

The night Nkanu fell ill, she went home to gather the documents and payments necessary to transport him back to the United States the next morning in an air ambulance. She left and Esege stayed at the hospital.

Esege, who retired from his work as a family physician in Baltimore when the twins were born, was still at the hospital when he looked at the report the hospital’s staff had prepared for the air ambulance company. He was shocked to see that it said Nkanu’s pupils were fixed and dilated. And on the Blantyre coma scale the doctors had marked their son at zero in a range of one to five, meaning he had shown no eye movement and didn’t respond to pain.

Egese’s voice cracked as he described his reaction to me: “Nobody said anything to me about this. I mean, this basically means Nkanu is gone.”

Not dead yet, but lacking any meaningful brain function. Esege said he believed, based on the report, that Dr. Majekodunmi knew Nkanu was beyond saving after the first cardiac arrest, but he didn’t want to tell Adichie because of his closeness to her and her family.

Esege said the doctor had urged him not to call Adichie until the hospital could do a CT scan, but he replied that he couldn’t keep the information from her. He texted his wife and asked her to come back, and she returned around midnight. In the next few hours, Nkanu’s heart stopped at least two more times.

“So they basically are doing cardiac resuscitations on this poor boy for more than four hours, until 8 in the morning, when they decided to call it,” Egese said. “Nkanu, our son, was gone.”

It seemed that Esege’s theory about the timing of Nkanu’s death was not one he had shared with his wife. Adichie looked at him, incredulous, and asked, “So, sorry. We don’t actually know when our son died?”

She paused and then said again, in disbelief, “We don’t know when he died.”

Turning to me, Adichie said, “I’m actually hearing this for the first time. Some of it.” She then referred to Esege by his nickname. “I didn’t know about IV’s conversation with the doctor when I went home to try to get the payments for the ambulance. I think IV’s tried to protect me.”

Near us in the dining room, Nkanu’s highchair was still at the table, next to his brother’s. His clothes were still folded upstairs in his room. Adichie mentioned that she now had to buy clothes for one boy, not two, but was still in the habit of adding two of every item — T-shirt, shorts, sweater — to the online shopping cart.

Intermittently, throughout our conversation, she took out her phone and showed me videos of Nkanu. For brief moments, there were echoes of his laughter. On the screen of his mother’s phone, Nkanu sang and danced, played with her jewelry and climbed on Esege’s back while he pretended to be a horse, galloping the child across imaginary fields.

Not long after Nkanu died, Adichie and Esege filed a complaint with the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria — a separate entity from the one conducting the inquest — and in February the council announced an initial finding of negligence on the part of three physicians: Dr. Majekodunmi; Dr. Titus Ogundare, the anesthesiologist who sedated Nkanu; and a doctor from Atlantis Pediatric Hospital, where Nkanu was first treated. The three were suspended pending a formal hearing; the Atlantis physician has since been cleared.

Dr. Ogundare did not respond to requests for comment.

The coroner’s inquest itself has turned into a battle, with Adichie accusing Euracare of playing a “monstrous cynical game” by creating unnecessary delays. (The inquest has been delayed until the fall.) When Esege joined an inquest hearing remotely in June, Euracare shocked the couple by accusing them of a crime: destroying evidence by having their son cremated. According to local news reports, the hospital’s lawyer, Taiwo Osipitan, said: “What they did is punishable by 15 years imprisonment. The issue is whether somebody who has done something wrong under the law can push for an inquest.”

Sylvester Shih, Euracare’s chief operating officer, did not respond to a request for comment.

“I feel so bad for IV,” Adichie said. “He’s on Zoom. He’s hearing it all. He’s hearing when someone is saying that he destroyed evidence, and by evidence, they mean our child.”

Even before Nkanu’s death, Adichie and Esege were adjusting to the losses of both of her parents and Esege’s brother in recent years. She recalled a conversation she had with her husband on Jan. 7, the day after Nkanu died.

“I just remember looking at IV and saying, ‘Do we have to have another funeral?’ IV said, ‘I cannot.’ And IV said, ‘We’ll cremate him. We’ll take him with us because we can’t leave him behind.’”

Along with her four novels Adichie has given popular TED talks and published short fiction, essays, children’s literature and, after her father’s death in 2020, a book called “Notes on Grief.”

“When my father died, I was struck by the physicality of grief. And this time, even more so,” she told me. “I feel it. It’s in my stomach and it’s in my chest, and you’re just so tired every day. Everything is difficult. Everything. And then you have to pretend. You have to pretend because you have children, and you’re terrified of how they’re doing. Sometimes my son doesn’t want me to hold him because I’m so weepy. He’s 2. So I really try. It feels like the full manifestation of my grief is impossible because of the condition of being a mother.”

About then, the little boy woke up with a wail and Esege went upstairs to get him.

Later, he swept into the room, his sister’s sweater draped over his shoulders like a superhero’s cape. He crawled into the cradle of his mother’s lap until he saw that his father had a soccer ball and went tearing after it. It was the week of the World Cup semifinals and the family found the games to be an engaging distraction.

Then the front door opened and the couple’s daughter bounced in. Tall like her father, she was dressed in all pink, her favorite color. She whispered something to her mother and Adichie smiled. Monday is hamburger day and her daughter wanted to make sure that even though she had eaten a burger over the weekend, she would get to have her favorite American meal because it was still Monday.

When we talked, Adichie had not been back to the country of her birth, the place she has brought to life in novels beloved by millions of readers, in six months. She had mentioned that she and Esege were planning to return there soon, and I asked if they planned to take their son and daughter with them. They have taught their children to love Nigeria even as they learn about its structural and political challenges.

Adichie grimaced and said, “They’re the reason we’re going.”

“Really, we’ve had two homes forever,” she continued. “We were in Nigeria every Christmas, every Easter, every summer. Our daughter said to me recently, ‘Mama, Nigeria is my happy place.’ She’s the one who wants to go.’”

I asked what her little boy understood about all that had happened. She shook her head and said, “He always says his brother is in Lagos.”

Adichie said she had always loved Nigeria and felt grateful to have a home there and one in Maryland. She came to the United States at 19 to study at Drexel University in Philadelphia and went on to earn master’s degrees from Johns Hopkins and Yale.

“I think that America made it possible for me to write, which is my life’s vocation,” she said. “But Nigeria gave me everything I needed to be able to write. And I feel grateful for that.”

But is Nigeria still where she is supposed to be?

She wiped the tears from her face and continued: “I mean, it is so surreal, all of this. I still can’t believe we’re talking about my son who died. You’re going through something, but you also feel like you’re outside of it.”

After a moment she said softly, “I do not want to go back to Nigeria.”

I came to this story with some experience of having a child who needed intensive medical care. When I wrote to Adichie and Esege about an interview, I let them know that I was a journalist but also a mother who spent four months in the NICU with my child.A few weeks later, I traveled to their home in Baltimore where the couple sat together, it turns out for the first time, and went hour by hour through the last night of their son’s life.

Deborah Segun (b. 1994) is a multidisciplinary artist from Lagos, Nigeria, based in London.

item.title: As Oil Prices Rise, BRICS Leaders Have What U.S. Doesn’t: Iran at the Table
item.description:
The summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies is designed to show what world leadership looks like when the West is not in the room.

And as widening clashes in the Middle East send global energy prices soaring, the gathering in New Delhi this weekend gives the leaders of China, India and Russia something Washington does not have: a seat at the table with Iran.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India is hosting the BRICS club — named after its earliest members, Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — that has been conceived as a counterweight to the West.

The Indian capital has largely been shut down for the meeting. Soldiers in khaki uniforms carrying rifles patrolled the streets, and steel road blocks cluttered the city center. Highways leading from the airport were also blanketed with BRICS signs depicting Mr. Modi alongside slogans such as: “Together we build, together we rise.”

That slogan points to the hope that the BRICS group has of projecting solidarity among its membership, which has expanded in recent years to include countries such as Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia. The message of unity stands in contrast to the global friction emanating from the Trump administration’s tariffs and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted global energy corridors.

In reality, expectations are low that BRICS, a loose bloc, will be able to step up to fill that gap in leadership, let alone broker a diplomatic off-ramp to the crisis in the Middle East.

The group has been split by tensions between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, a U.S. security partner that has been targeted by thousands of Iranian ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones since the war started in February. Divisions prevented the group from producing a joint statement in May after a meeting of BRICS foreign ministers. (The U.A.E. sent Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the crown prince of Abu Dhabi, who arrived on Friday.)

“The world is really rapidly fracturing, and in theory that’s really kind of what the BRICS have been saying all along,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin. “But they’re really wildly underperforming.”

“It’s very difficult to have such a big and expanded club of countries that are united by their animosity to Western hegemony but have very different interests, sometimes opposing each other, sometimes at war with each other,” he added.

Both President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran, whose countries are mired in wars and under fierce pressure from the West in the form of sanctions, moved quickly on Friday to press their agendas even before the summit started.

Mr. Pezeshkian criticized U.S. power and urged fellow members to build alternative financial tools to protect themselves from Western pressure. “Who said it should decide for the entire world, that others have no rights, and that whatever they want everyone else has to obey?” he said in a speech. “This is something we will not accept.”

Mr. Modi, however, used a meeting with Mr. Pezeshkian on Friday to deliver a pointed message, urging him to safeguard “freedom of navigation and commerce” — a tacit reference to the chokeholds on the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea that threaten India’s own fuel imports.

That messaging is the kind of global leadership that Mr. Modi wants to be seen exercising. He does not share the same opposition to the West as Mr. Putin and Mr. Pezeshkian, embodying instead India’s historical preference for nonalignment and strategic friendships with powers from across the ideological spectrum. India’s chief rival for influence in the group is China, which has sought to use BRICS to displace U.S. power.

The summit is an opportunity for Mr. Modi to burnish his statesman credentials at a time when his political power at home has weakened and the Indian economy continues to take a back seat to China’s.

The Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, arrived for the summit on Saturday, but officials have not said if he will meet with Mr. Pezeshkian.

Iran is Beijing’s closest strategic partner in the Middle East, but China also has economic ties with Persian Gulf states that have been targeted by Iranian strikes.

At a recent regional security summit in Kyrgyzstan, Mr. Xi and Mr. Pezeshkian met only briefly on the sidelines rather than in a separate bilateral meeting.

That fueled speculation that Beijing was unhappy over the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Mr. Xi could have also been distancing himself from Tehran to avoid provoking President Trump, whom he is scheduled to meet in Washington later this month.

“A substantive bilateral meeting in New Delhi would therefore carry significance well beyond protocol,” said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.

“It could help clarify whether China still sees Iran as a strategic partner worth investing political capital in at a moment of acute pressure, or whether Beijing is increasingly keeping Tehran at arm’s length,” Mr. Azizi said.

Perhaps more important to China is Mr. Xi’s meeting with Mr. Modi later in the day.

Mr. Xi’s visit is the first he has made to India in seven years, and is a sign of the continued stabilization of relations between Beijing and New Delhi. Ties hit a low in 2020 following a clash of Indian and Chinese forces in a disputed border region.

Other leaders arriving in New Delhi brought their own awkward entanglements with the group’s Western-skeptic tilt.

President Cyril Ramaphosa of South Africa shares Mr. Modi’s preference for using BRICS to build relationships across the globe. But the coalition has also created diplomatic headaches for Pretoria.

In January, South Africa was criticized by the Trump administration for allowing Iran to participate in BRICS naval drills off the South African coast at a time when the Iranian government faced accusations of fatally crushing street protests in Iran.

Mr. Ramaphosa said that China was running the exercises and that South African waters were chosen because of the convenient location.

South African officials have been disappointed that the bloc has not been able to reach consensus opinions on divisive conflicts like the wars in Iran and Gaza, said David Africa, an international relations analyst based in Cape Town.

“South Africa has knocked its head and realizes it won’t extract much diplomatically on the issues it’s concerned about,” Mr. Africa said. Instead, he said, South Africa is likely to focus on economic issues like trade, business and development at the summit.

One of the BRICS group’s most ambitious economic goals is to reduce global reliance on the dollar.

“De-dollarization,” as the effort is known, would throw a lifeline to countries like Russia and Iran, which have struggled to pay for imported goods since the United States and other Western countries restricted their access to the dollar.

The dollar’s status as the world’s reserve currency is an “exorbitant privilege” for the United States, economists say — and it’s a privilege that Mr. Trump intends to keep. At the start of his second term, he wrote that any country trying to “create a new BRICS Currency” to circumvent the dollar could “say goodbye to selling into the beautiful U.S. economy.”

An alternative reserve currency is not realistic at this point. But many countries that benefit from having the dollar as the world’s standard legal tender — India, for instance, which fears a financial future dominated by China — still want to see its dominance decrease. India has proposed that BRICS countries should link their banking systems more directly, allowing them to pay debts to one another without converting sums into dollars.

It is already buying oil from Russia using rupees and rubles.

Reporting was contributed by Valerie Hopkins in Moscow, Rania Khaled in Cairo, John Eligon in Johannesburg and Yeganeh Torbati in Istanbul.

item.title: U.S. and Brazil Partnered in Fighting Crime. A Diplomatic Spat Threatens That.
item.description:
A diplomatic rift is hindering cooperation between the United States and Brazil on jointly fighting organized crime, according to U.S. and Brazilian officials, an issue the Trump administration has placed at the center of its agenda in the Western Hemisphere.

The State Department is withholding visas for two Brazilian federal police agents assigned to posts in the United States, where they would be working with U.S. Homeland Security Investigations and other federal agencies to combat transnational crimes, according to one American and three senior Brazilian officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

In response, Brazil is now also blocking the visa of a U.S. law enforcement official meant to be stationed in the country, according to the American and Brazilian officials.

The U.S. government, citing a busy agenda, also declined a request for a visit by Brazilian customs and revenue agents investigating money laundering and arms smuggling by international drug gangs, according to two other Brazilian officials.

Brazil and the United States have a long history of jointly investigating international crimes, like fraud and trafficking, and sending law enforcement officials to each other’s countries. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an attaché in Brazil for over two decades.

In the past, joint action by Brazil and the United States has helped the authorities dismantle international corruption schemes, piracy networks and human trafficking rings.

That type of close cooperation, experts say, is becoming crucial for fighting Latin America’s drug gangs, which have more resources and greater geographic reach than ever before.

“Today, criminal factions know no borders,” said Edvandir Felix de Paiva, the president of Brazil’s association of federal police commissioners. “So we need to be working together.”

The recent disruptions in cooperation, which have not been previously reported, come against a backdrop of strained relations over the past year, stemming from President Trump’s attempts to meddle in Brazil’s internal affairs. This rift has only deepened in recent months with the administration’s apparent readiness to help Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate challenging President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist, in Brazil’s elections in October.

Fighting transnational gangs has become a top priority for the Trump administration, and, in that fight, it has joined forces with Latin American countries led by conservative leaders. But fraying diplomatic ties may be derailing cooperation between the United States and Brazil, the Western Hemisphere’s most populous nations.

“The perception is that U.S. security policy toward Brazil has become entangled in politics,” said Robert Muggah, a security expert and research director of the Igarapé Institute, a Brazil-based research institution. “It hasn’t led to a fundamental rupture,” he added, “but it has introduced new complexities into the relationship and shaded it with levels of mistrust.”

The State Department declined to comment on the specifics of the visas, but said in a statement that the Trump administration was protecting “the nation and its citizens by upholding the highest standards of national security and public safety through our visa process.” The department added that it would continue working with Brazil to advance “longstanding shared interests.”

The U.S. Customs and Border Protection said in a statement it was committed to engaging with Brazilian authorities to advance “security goals and disrupt transnational crime.”

Brazil’s federal police and Foreign Ministry declined to comment. The Finance Ministry, which oversees the nation’s customs, revenue and border control agency, said the two nations maintain a dialogue aimed at exchanging best practices and combating transnational crime.

The two Brazilian federal police agents who have not been granted visas were scheduled to take their posts in Miami and New York last month, according to the Brazilian officials. They had already been selected and vetted by U.S. and Brazilian authorities early this year as part of a routine personnel change, one of the officials said.

One of the federal police attachés was to replace Marcelo Ivo de Carvalho, who was expelled from the United States in April and accused by the Trump administration of a “political witch hunt” over his role in the arrest of a former Brazilian intelligence chief. The chief ​had fled to the United States after he was convicted of plotting a coup in his home country with the former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The elder Mr. Bolsonaro, an ally of Mr. Trump’s, is serving a 27-year sentence over his attempt to cling to power. In response to Mr. Carvalho’s expulsion, Brazil revoked the credentials of a U.S. law enforcement agent working in Brasília, the capital.

In another reciprocal move, Brazil is now withholding a visa for the U.S. law enforcement agent’s successor until its own police attachés are allowed to take up their U.S. posts, according to two senior Brazilian officials. The authorities in both countries are still in negotiations over the visas, American and Brazilian officials said.

A team of nearly a dozen agents from Brazil’s customs and revenue agency also asked to visit their U.S. counterparts in Washington in June, as part of a recent push to increase cooperation in countering transnational money laundering and smuggling operations. But U.S. authorities declined their request, citing a crowded agenda through November, the two Brazilian officials said.

Under a new intelligence-sharing system introduced this year, customs agents in each country were alerting each other about suspicious container shipments, helping U.S. and Brazilian authorities to intercept illicit cargo, such as weapons, according to one of the officials.

While police and intelligence experts say this kind of technical cooperation between Brazil and the United States continues, a lack of high-level coordination may thwart more ambitious plans.

While Brazil does not export significant quantities of drugs to the United States, it is a major transit route for cocaine heading to Europe, Africa and elsewhere. Brazilian gangs are also increasingly forging alliances with Mexican and Colombian gangs and finding new ways to smuggle drugs out of Latin America.

Experts say Brazilian organized criminal groups use the U.S. banking system to launder profits from illicit activities. The United States is also a key source for these groups of illegal arms, smuggled from U.S. states with permissive gun laws. Last month, Brazilian police arrested two men in connection with weapons parts mailed from Florida.

During multiple meetings and phone calls over the past year, including as recently as Aug. 21, Mr. Lula has pitched Mr. Trump on closer cooperation on combating organized crime.

At a White House meeting in May, Mr. Lula delivered a proposal on how the two countries could fight drug gangs together by targeting their weapons and finances, according to a Brazilian official. The Trump administration never responded to the proposal, the official said.

That same month, the United States moved to designate the country’s two largest drug gangs as terrorist organizations after aggressive lobbying by Mr. Bolsonaro and his allies, who have accused Mr. Lula of being weak on crime. Public security is a major concern for many Brazilians and a key issue in October’s presidential election.

The full effect of the U.S. designation is not yet clear, but it has already led to at least one policing stumble. The United States used the designation to apply sanctions to people who had secretly been under investigation by Brazilian police, revealing their links to gangs and tipping them off to the probe. As a result, Brazilian police had to rush to arrest the targets.

At the same time, Washington has sought to strengthen cooperation with conservative leaders in the Western Hemisphere through the Shield of the Americas, a new security alliance against drug traffickers that does not include Brazil. Some members, including Ecuador and Colombia, have agreed to joint military operations with the United States in their countries.

Last month, Brazil was also not invited to a U.S.-led gathering of security officials from Latin America and the Caribbean at the United Nations.

The diplomatic scuffle between Brazil and the United States escalated in recent months, with a series of other visa rejections and cancellations. But while the Trump administration has sought to use visas as part of its effort to assert its dominance in Latin America, this approach may only further alienate Brazil.

“We want to have Brazil closer to the United States — not further away,” said Jimmy Story, a former U.S. ambassador and a founding partner of Global Frontier Advisors, a consulting firm. “And this kind of diplomacy has the opposite effect.”

Alice Maciel and Thayz Guimarães contributed reporting from Brasília.

item.title: ‘We Left in the Clothes We Were Wearing’: Yemenis Flee New Fighting
item.description:
At least half of the population is hungry. Millions of children are unvaccinated. A measles outbreak is spreading.

The people of Yemen have survived the indignities of a more than decade-long civil war. This past week, many were again running for their lives.

A new round of fighting has erupted between the Houthis, the Iran-backed militia in the north, and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, widening the regional conflict that began early this year with the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran.

More than 46,000 people fled their homes in the past week alone, a U.N. agency estimated on Friday, some with little more than the clothes on their backs.

Al-Megdad Hashem and his family were among them. At first, one night late last week, they stayed home, kept awake by the sound of shelling. Then, the next morning, shells landed near their house, in the fiercely contested province of Taiz, wounding two people, including Mr. Hashem’s nephew.

The only way to get them to a hospital was to load them onto a truck that normally carries construction materials. All told, he said, 34 people piled in, including Mr. Hashem, his wife, their four children and his elderly parents. They had barely enough time to stuff their belongings into one small bag.

“It was difficult to take anything,” he said. “We want the war to stop so that people can return to their homes.”

The civil war had largely settled into a fragile peace in recent years, since a 2022 U.N.-brokered cease-fire effectively partitioned the country between government- and Houthi-held areas. Now, Yemen is again in the throes of full-fledged fighting, aggravating what was already one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Making matters worse, the U.N. World Food Program is so short of money that it has suspended food aid altogether and reduced its provision of monthly cash assistance to every other month, Carl Skau, the agency’s acting executive director, said in a phone interview on Thursday. He had visited Yemen last week.

Children were not going to school in the camps for displaced people that he visited, he said. Yemenis told him they were selling their belongings to buy food. And at one health clinic, a long line of mothers were waiting to be seen, with malnourished children in their arms. “They were struggling to afford one meal a day,” he said.

Yemen, he said, has been barraged not only by the fighting. The disruption of shipping in the region has also raised food prices in a country that imports most of what it eats. Meanwhile, droughts and floods have damaged Yemen’s farms. “The little they produce inside is turned upside down by the weather,” Mr. Skau said.

Even before the latest surge in violence, an estimated 4.5 million Yemenis were displaced from their homes. Nearly half of the country’s health facilities are not functional. Attacks on aid workers have forced the United Nations to suspend operations in the Houthi-held north.

This week, Houthi forces captured Mokha, a strategic Red Sea port city in Taiz, as well as an island in the waterway, according to two Yemeni officials, giving the militia a foothold in Bab al-Mandab, a major maritime choke point through which oil from Saudi Arabia passes on its way to Asia.

Houthi forces have also attacked Saudi oil facilities, in turn pushing up already rising global oil prices.

The Houthis have frequently accused Saudi Arabia of striking their positions.

On Friday, the broadcaster Al-Masirah, which is controlled by the militia, said that Saudi Arabia had launched two rounds of airstrikes on the port of Mokha. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Nations said on Thursday that at least 14 civilians were killed in the fighting this past week, including two children.

Last Saturday, in the contested Maqbanah district of Taiz Province, Omar Abdulaziz al-Himyari, 25, fled after hearing shelling nearby. At dawn, he and five family members climbed for two hours by foot to a mountain ridge, their route to the closest road. From there they found a car to the nearest city.

“We left in the clothes we were wearing,” he said. “We couldn’t carry anything because of the situation and the difficult terrain.”

They left behind all of their most valuable belongings, including their cows and goats, their beehives and the grain they had planted in their fields.

For now, Mr. al-Himyari is staying with his brother-in-law and looking for work in the city of Taiz, now crowded with the newly displaced. The prices of flour and rice have shot up at the market. Water must be procured from a tanker, and that too is pricey.

“I honestly don’t know how we will manage our daily needs,” he said.

More than 18 million Yemenis face what the United Nations calls acute food insecurity, with 2.2 million children acutely malnourished.

Disease and medical care also remain pressing concerns. The World Health Organization reported more than 17,600 measles cases in the first seven months of the year. At the main hospital in the government-held city of Marib, maternity and obstetric services have been suspended to make space for trauma care, the W.H.O. said, and dead bodies exceed “available mortuary capacity.”

The crisis is especially dire in the Houthi-held north. United Nations operations have been suspended there since October, when U.N. and other aid workers were detained and U.N. offices were raided by the militia. Seventy-three U.N. staff members remain in Houthi detention, the U.N. relief chief told the Security Council in August.

And although Yemen was once a focus of world aid groups, many major funders of relief, such as the United States, have significantly cut their aid budgets.

Yemen needs $2.2 billion in humanitarian assistance, according to the U.N. relief agency, which said it had received only 20 percent of that.

item.title: In Flood-Stricken Nepal, a Cool Gust Carries Hopes of a Miracle Rescue
item.description:
Deep beneath the Himalayas, six men were harnessing the fierce force of glacial melt that provides electricity to Nepal when a terrible deluge struck, filling their workplace, an underground powerhouse, with a churn of silt, rock and water. Floor by floor, life was extinguished.

But two and a half weeks after that devastating flooding, rescue crews digging through a silt-swamped tunnel at the Chilime hydropower project have made a tantalizing discovery. The area toward the top of the five-floor underground facility appears to be fed by a pocket of air.

In a drowned and battered landscape, the presence of oxygen, cool and fresh according to rescue workers, lit faint hopes that the six workers — the only ones still unaccounted for at the facility — might have somehow survived.

Chances of life are still slim. While three workers were pulled out of tunnels at other hydropower projects on the ninth and 10th days after the floods, another week has now passed. The floods have killed at least 1,385 people in Nepal and left 5,130 missing, along with hundreds more unaccounted for in neighboring Tibet.

Still, for days, rescue crews brought in by helicopter — Nepali and Indian soldiers, veteran mountaineers, Australian engineers and locals who had themselves lost relatives to the natural disaster — clawed through the silt by hand, sometimes crouching on planks to prevent the earth from claiming them, too. Efforts to pump out the sludge failed. Roads and bridges in the mountainous region were washed away, so heavy machinery could not be brought in to excavate the tunnel until Friday, 17 days after the floods.

“My heart is breaking for the six workers, and we have to do everything to try to save them, if there is even a small, small chance,” said Kulman Ghising, the former managing director of the Chilime Hydropower Company, who has lent his expertise to the recovery effort.

More than 900 hydropower workers are dead or missing from the floods, which appear to have been caused by a plummeting chunk of glacier and bedrock. Fourteen hydropower projects were destroyed, along with a large solar power station. Roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s electricity generation was wiped out, in a country that counts hydropower as one of its major exports.

Mr. Ghising, who, as the longtime head of the Nepal Electricity Authority, presided over the rapid electrification of one of Asia’s poorest nations, said he had personally hired one of the six men who is believed to be trapped in the powerhouse. He also helped build six hydropower projects in the region.

“In one, two moments, everything is gone, everything we built for decades,” he said.

The rush of water, debris and mud from the Trishuli River in Nepal swept into the 820-foot tunnel to Chilime’s underground powerhouse, choking it shut. As of Saturday night, the crews had fully cleared about 200 feet of the tunnel, with a route in the upper part excavated deeper. For days, they had used buckets, shovels and bare hands, “digging like a rabbit,” according to Manish Bista, the plant manager.

Then, on Friday night, heavy machinery brought via a newly cleared road finally started to move earth in the tunnel. But hours later, a wheel loader tumbled over. Another machine suffered a flat tire. Most supplies are still flown in by helicopters landing on a perilous patch of riverside.

“We are isolated on all sides,” said Baburaja Maharjan, the current managing director of Chilime Hydropower, who has been at the rescue site since the day the flood struck. “We have no spare parts or machines. We have very limited resources.”

The teams are now working 24 hours a day, with no way out if another big flood were to come, Mr. Maharjan said.

But late this week, a breakthrough spurred on the exhausted rescue crews.

As Nepali Army soldiers crawled into a crevice in the muck, about 350 feet into the tunnel, they felt a gust of cool air through a tiny gap. Yelling into the space, they heard an echo and determined that there was an air pocket ahead.

One tunnel in the underground network slopes upward and connects to the top floor of the powerhouse. Rescue crews think that this tunnel may be free of debris as it inclines. Mr. Maharjan said that during emergencies, the engineers stationed in the powerhouse have been trained to run from their computer stations one story below to an assembly point on the top floor. That area may also have access to filtered water and a basic kitchen, where workers usually cooked their instant noodles or rice and lentils.

“There is some hope of life inside,” Mr. Maharjan said. “That is why we are continuing with extremely difficult work.”

Saroj Pandey is one of the six workers who was on duty in the powerhouse when the deluge came, according to Chilime directors and engineers.

Mr. Pandey, a computer engineer, was married two years ago and welcomed his first child last year, according to friends. One of them, Swoorup Joshi, lives in Australia and used to spend hours video chatting with Mr. Pandey, playing guitar or just talking about life.

Hours before the flood, Mr. Joshi texted his friend a single word: “Bro.”

Mr. Pandey did not respond.

“He’s just a chill, happy guy,” said Mr. Joshi, who created a website to document the efforts to locate the missing men. “I can’t imagine he’s gone.”

item.title: Death Toll From Ferry Fire in the Philippines Rises to 76
item.description:
Emergency workers have recovered the remains of dozens more people who died when a passenger ferry caught fire in the Philippines, bringing the death toll to 76, the country’s Coast Guard said on Saturday.

The ferry, the June Aster, was carrying 132 people, including 17 crew members, from Manila to Coron, an island in Palawan Province, when a fire broke out on board on Wednesday. Over the next two days, rescue workers first found five bodies, and then 30 more. Their efforts were hampered by conditions at sea that caused the vessel to drift nearly eight nautical miles away from its initial distress location.

On Saturday, the death toll climbed again when rescuers recovered 41 more bodies, Commodore Noemi Cayabyab, a Philippine Coast Guard spokeswoman, said in a statement. There are 43 survivors, but 13 people still remain unaccounted for, she added.

“This figure may still change as recovery and identification operations continue,” she said, noting that two people listed on the passenger manifest had not boarded the vessel.

The authorities are still investigating the cause of the blaze. The ferry, which left the Baseco port area in Manila, the capital, was scheduled to arrive at 6 p.m. Wednesday in Coron, a popular diving destination known for its limestone cliffs and clear waters. At approximately 6:45 p.m., when the June Aster was nearing the village of Marcilla on Coron Island, a fire broke out.

Surviving passengers described thick black smoke and screams in the ensuing chaos. Rescue workers found victims still inside the vessel, while other bodies floated in the water, witnesses said.

Maritime accidents occur frequently in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands. In January, at least 65 people died after a ferry sank in the southern part of the country.

item.title: Saudi Arabia’s Oil ‘Lifeline’ Was Attacked. Here’s What to Know.
item.description:
Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s biggest oil producers, on Friday said it had shut down a vital oil pipeline as a precautionary measure following a drone attack from Iraqi territory.

The infrastructure, known as the East-West pipeline, is key to Saudi Arabia’s ability to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz — the Persian Gulf waterway that Iran blockaded after the U.S.-Israeli attack in late February, throttling global oil exports.

The targeting of the East-West pipeline showed that even alternatives to the strait can be disrupted if Iran and its proxies expand their attacks, exposing another vulnerability in efforts to restore the flow of oil to world markets and bring down energy prices.

Here is what you need to know about the pipeline.

Built in the 1980s — when the Iran-Iraq war was similarly squeezing oil exports from the Persian Gulf — the 1,201-kilometer (746-mile) pipeline crosses the Arabian Peninsula to the Saudi port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.

Earlier this summer, Yasir O. Al-Rumayyan, the chairman of Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil company, said engineers had expanded the pipeline’s capacity to carry up to seven million barrels per day, nearly 30 percent more than before the war.

“We had a similar situation back in the ’80s where the Strait of Hormuz was threatened to be blockaded by the Iranian regime,” Mr. Al-Rumayyan said in June. “It was decided since then that we will have a pipeline from east to west and if it wasn’t for this pipeline, we wouldn’t have a lifeline for us as a Saudi economy.”

Still, Saudi Arabia’s oil exports fell last month to 3.2 million barrels a day, the lowest level in at least 13 years, according to data from Kpler, a maritime information company.

The pipeline has allowed Saudi Arabia to mitigate the impact of the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz by keeping oil flowing out through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern entry to the Red Sea.

But that backup route has come under threat as well.

In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized new territory and tried to cut off the Red Sea to Saudi shipping by declaring a blockade and by firing on Saudi vessels. In the past week, the Houthis have taken over more coastal territory near the strait, including the Perim Island in the Red Sea and the port of Mokha, further threatening Saudi vessels carrying oil from the East-West pipeline down the Red Sea to global markets.

Saudi Arabia can also export its oil north out of the Red Sea though a pipeline near the Suez Canal, in Egypt. But that route through the Mediterranean is costlier and adds weeks to the voyage to Asia, where most of the kingdom’s customers are.

Over the past several weeks, a growing number of oil tankers have also been avoiding the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz with U.S. military guidance. The number is still a fraction of those that transited the waterway before the war, though, according to shipping trackers — meaning the pipeline is still important.

No group has officially claimed the drone attack on the East-West pipeline, although on Saturday, President Trump said Iran was “probably” behind the assault. Iran has not commented on the claim.

Saudi officials have said the drone came from Iraq, which has been a hotbed for well-armed militias under Tehran’s sway that the Iraqi government has struggled to bring under control. On Saturday, the office of Iraq’s prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, said he had agreed to conduct a joint investigation with Iran into drone launches along the Iraqi border.

Analysts have said that a broadening U.S. economic campaign against Iran was likely to lead it to escalate attacks in the region and try to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.

“Saudi Arabia had the workaround, at least partially, through this East-West pipeline,,” said Joey Hood, a former senior State Department official. “Iran saw that and said — we’re getting the economic stranglehold around our necks, so we’ve got to do something.”

“Seeing the Iranians doing such bold and outlandish things seems to signal that the economic strangulation is beginning to work,” he added.

The attack on Friday is the first against the pipeline since it was targeted in April. At the time, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said a drone had hit a pumping station and led to the loss of nearly 700,000 barrels per day of pumping capacity. While the pipeline was quickly brought back online, it exposed a fundamental vulnerability for Saudi Arabia’s oil routes as it seeks to bypass the volatility of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

Following that attack, and after months of restraint, Saudi Arabia joined the United States in bombing Iran-linked Iraqi militias in July, targeting logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq.

This time, Saudi Arabia has “chosen not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government” in preventing future attacks from its territory, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.

But Mr. Hood, the former diplomat, said Iran was likely to continue its attacks, which could ultimately force Gulf states like Saudi Arabia to take a more aggressive stance.

“This conflict is continuing to widen,” he said. “The Gulf countries have shown extraordinary restraint, but I don’t think that lasts forever.”

Lisa Friedman contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Says Irish Unification Would Be ‘Fantastic,’ Breaking With Precedent
item.description:
Shortly after setting foot in Dublin, President Trump on Saturday said it would be “fantastic” if Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland unified, breaking with decades of U.S. neutrality on an issue rooted in a long history of violence.

“I don’t want to cause any problem. I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Mr. Trump said in Dublin alongside Micheál Martin, Ireland’s taoiseach, or prime minister. “It’s going to happen eventually.”

He later seemed to acknowledge that he had stepped into a politically problematic topic.

The American president said he still believed it would “be a cool thing” if Northern Ireland broke away from the United Kingdom, but joked that half the room would clear out after hearing his remarks.

“No matter how well you say it, there’s no good answer,” Mr. Trump told a crowd of embassy employees and business leaders gathered at Deerfield Residence, where the U.S. ambassador lives.

The United States has long supported the U.S.-brokered 1998 Belfast Agreement, also known as the Good Friday Agreement, which ended roughly three decades of violence between those seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain a part of the United Kingdom.

Part of that deal was that Northern Ireland would remain part of the United Kingdom until a majority of its people voted otherwise in a referendum.

In keeping with his freewheeling approach to the global stage, Mr. Trump has mused about the unification of Ireland before. Earlier this year, he suggested there should be a “merger” between Northern Ireland and Ireland because of how well Mr. Martin got along with Northern Ireland’s deputy first minister, Emma Little-Pengelly. She later said the comment was made in jest and should not be taken seriously.

Mr. Trump’s comment on Saturday came just days after Andy Burnham, the recently elected British prime minister, said there was not enough public support for a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom and until there was “there will not be one.” Mr. Trump himself acknowledged on Saturday that the government in London would most likely “have something to say about” about his comments on reunification.

Patrick Dwyer-Cummins, a spokesman for 10 Downing Street, said that Mr. Burnham’s position remained unchanged and he was committed to upholding the Good Friday Agreement.

But Mr. Trump’s comment did indeed prompt some immediate criticism.

Gavin Robinson, the leader of Northern Ireland’s main pro-union party, said on social media that “President Trump knows better than most that elections matter.”

“Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington,” he said. “Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people.”

The reference to reunification was not the only unconventional aspect of Mr. Trump’s remarks.

American presidents, when speaking overseas, typically have refrained from lacing into their domestic rivals. But Mr. Trump used his speech in Dublin to repeatedly attack Democrats, including describing former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., who has cancer, as physically infirm. Mr. Biden, who has Irish ancestry, traveled to Northern Ireland in 2023 to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement.

item.title: Iran Finds Escalation Is a Fruitful Path to Leverage in War With U.S.
item.description:
The routes to export oil out of the Middle East are diminishing. The price of energy is soaring. And Iran’s neighbors could be about to endorse some measure of its authority over the Strait of Hormuz.

In the past week, Iran and its allies have used military escalation to upend any minimal sense of stability in the region, most dramatically in Yemen. That is shifting the momentum in Iran’s war with the United States to its advantage.

The shift may not be decisive. The Islamic republic remains under immense economic pressure, with the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of its southern ports and escalating rounds of sanctions cutting it off from the world.

And yet, a series of attacks in recent days by Iran and its allies have expanded the scope of the conflict. That, analysts said, may have given Tehran greater leverage, at least at this moment.

The Iranian-allied Houthis of Yemen captured a Red Sea island on Friday, giving them a perch to disrupt shipping in another critical waterway for shipping oil out of the Middle East.

“The Houthi success in Yemen has swung the pendulum back in Iran’s favor,” said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group. Iran, he said, had managed to shift “the status quo without bringing back a return to full-scale war, which the regime likely doesn’t want at this time.”

While Iran backs the Houthis with weapons, cash and logistics, analysts say the Shiite militant group is neither a direct conduit for Iranian interests in Yemen nor fully independent of Tehran’s influence.

The price of oil briefly jumped to about $110 per barrel on Friday, roughly 50 percent above prewar levels. That gives Iran further leverage, as high energy prices pose a political risk for President Trump as his party heads into elections in the fall.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, has become increasingly reliant on the Red Sea, since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz early in the war. But the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships in July, firing on passing vessels in the Red Sea and attacking oil facilities in the kingdom.

Oil exports from Saudi Arabia plunged last month to their lowest level in at least 13 years. Compounding its problems, a pipeline that carries oil to the kingdom’s Red Sea ports was temporarily shut down on Friday after a drone attack from inside Iraqi territory, the Saudi energy ministry said.

While it was unclear who was behind the attack, Saudi Arabia has in the past accused Iran-backed militias in Iraq of attacking its energy infrastructure, and Mr. Trump said on Saturday that Iran was “probably” responsible.

Since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February, the longstanding U.S. security guarantee for its Gulf allies has looked less assured, with those countries coming under missile and drone attacks from Iranian forces.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia urged Mr. Trump to take military action against the Houthis, but the president said he was not willing to do so, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations. Mr. Trump said Saturday that the Houthis had conveyed to his administration that they do not want a fight with the United States.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains far below what it was before the war, though a limited number of ships had been getting through with the help of U.S. naval escorts.

That meant Iran was losing some leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, said Behnam Ben Taleblu, an expert on Iran at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank that is hawkish on Iran. “The regime is now clawing it back elsewhere,” he said, with its allies staging attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

“Iran’s military strategy is both escalatory and predictable,” Mr. Taleblu said. “It’s all about cross-domain escalation for an increasingly risk-tolerant Tehran.”

Iran has also been stepping up attacks against U.S. warships patrolling the Persian Gulf. Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s top national security official, said that Iran had tested what he called its first anti-ship missile against a U.S. ship. The U.S. military responded to Iranian attacks on its warships by destroying several Iranian crude oil carriers.

Iran’s attacks were highly risky, Mr. Taleblu said.

“These high and fast-flying systems can be fired from further inland and, if they strike a U.S. vessel, could cause a significant loss of life,” he said.

Iran’s actions in the region complicated the BRICS summit of emerging economies in New Delhi this weekend, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India urging Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, to safeguard “freedom of navigation and commerce.” India’s own fuel imports are threatened by the ongoing conflict.

Mr. Pezeshkian used his speech at one of the summit’s events to criticize American power.

“Who said it should decide for the entire world, that others have no rights, and that whatever they want everyone else has to obey?” he said. “This is something we will not accept.”

In what could be a potentially powerfully symbolic image of how Tehran’s asymmetric military strategy has resulted in concrete wins, Iran and Oman are set to meet on Monday with other Persian Gulf states to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman said on Friday.

Omani officials did not respond on Friday to a request for comment about the meeting. For weeks, Iranian and Omani officials have been discussing a shared agreement for managing the strait, though Iran has insisted that even such an agreement would not mean that the strait is fully reopen for shipping traffic.

It was still unclear what may come out of the meeting, if it takes place at all. Bahrain, a Gulf country that has been attacked by Iran and hosts a major U.S. military base, said on Saturday that it would not take part. Other Gulf countries do not appear to have immediately commented publicly.

The meeting, if it goes ahead, is “a reflection of the profound disappointment across the Gulf with Washington and with U.S. policy in the region,” Danny Citrinowicz, a retired Israeli intelligence officer who specializes in Iran, said on social media.

They were being forced to choose, Mr. Citrinowicz said, “between an open-ended confrontation with no clear political endgame, one that is destabilizing the region and inflicting enormous economic costs,” and some degree of recognition of Iran’s authority over the strait in hopes of restoring stability.

Iran’s diplomacy with the Gulf countries is “a textbook case of a knife in the back and a handshake in the front,” Mr. Taleblu said. “Tehran spent months attacking these nations directly and indirectly and creating the conditions that led to a major loss of revenue and inability to export oil.”

Now, he said, it is trying to “lock in a more favorable posture of deference to Tehran from elements of the American order in the region.”
